Vitamin B12 - Health Professional Fact Sheet

content.text:
For most people, **there isn’t a clearly defined “too much” amount of vitamin B12**: the NIH has **not set a tolerable upper intake limit** because B12 has low toxicity and excess is often excreted in urine. The adult recommended intake is only **2.4 mcg/day**, but supplements commonly contain **500–1,000+ mcg** because absorption is limited. ([ods.od.nih.gov](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminB12-HealthProfessional/?uid=c273e26eea9a1s16&utm_source=openai))

That said, **more isn’t automatically better**:

- **Typical daily need:** ~**2.4 mcg/day** for most adults; higher needs can apply in pregnancy/breastfeeding or deficiency. ([ods.od.nih.gov](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminB12-HealthProfessional/?uid=c273e26eea9a1s16&utm_source=openai))  
- **Common supplement doses:** **500–1,000 mcg/day** are often used, especially if deficient or at risk.  
- **High-dose B12** can sometimes cause side effects like **acne/skin rash, nausea, diarrhea, headache, dizziness**, or interactions/concerns depending on your health situation. Mayo Clinic advises talking with a clinician before high-dose supplements, especially with medications. ([mayoclinic.org](https://www.mayoclinic.org/drugs-supplements-vitamin-b12/art-20363663?p=1&utm_source=openai))  
- **High B12 on a blood test** isn’t always from “taking too much”; it can also be associated with certain medical conditions, so it’s worth discussing with a healthcare provider if your level is unexpectedly high. ([my.clevelandclinic.org](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/high-b12-levels?utm_source=openai))

**Practical rule of thumb:**  
If you’re not deficient and don’t have a risk factor — vegan/vegetarian diet, older age, metformin use, acid-reducing meds, gastric surgery, malabsorption — a daily mega-dose like **1,000–5,000 mcg** may be unnecessary. If you’re taking more than **1,000 mcg/day long-term**, or getting injections without a diagnosis, it’s reasonable to check with your clinician and consider a B12 level ± methylmalonic acid test.

If you tell me your **dose**, **form** — pill, sublingual, injection — and why you’re taking it, I can help put it in context.
